faq.a: It indicates weakness of the gluteus medius/minimus, often from hip osteoarthritis or nerve injury.

exam: A 28‑year‑old motorcyclist presents after a collision with a shortened, internally rotated left leg – what is your immediate management and why? — Recognise posterior dislocation, perform gentle traction‑reduction, protect sciatic nerve, obtain urgent X‑ray.

A child with fever and hip pain has a normal AP pelvis X‑ray. Which bedside test helps you decide on joint aspiration? — Perform hip ultrasound for effusion; if positive, aspirate to rule out septic arthritis.

During a ward round you note a patient with sickle cell disease and chronic groin pain; X‑ray shows femoral head flattening. What is the likely diagnosis and its long‑term risk? — Avascular necrosis; risk of secondary osteoarthritis and collapse.
Explain why the hip joint is more stable than the shoulder despite similar ball‑and‑socket design. — Deep acetabular socket, strong capsule, and robust ligamentous reinforcement limit dislocation.

A patient on long‑term steroids presents with hip pain; what imaging sequence should you follow and why? — Start with plain X‑ray; if normal but suspicion remains, obtain MRI to detect early osteonecrosis.
What clinical sign distinguishes intra‑articular from extra‑articular hip pathology? — Pain on passive internal rotation with hip flexed 90° points to intra‑articular disease.
In a low‑resource hospital without CT, how would you assess a suspected acetabular fracture? — Use AP pelvis X‑ray; look for disrupted Shenton’s line and asymmetry of the teardrop figure.
Why is the lateral femoral circumflex artery less important for femoral head viability in adults? — It supplies the neck and capsule, not the head; the medial circumflex artery is the primary source.
ai.title: Hip Joint Anatomy
related: Avascular Necrosis of the Femoral Head
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The hip is a deep ball‑and‑socket joint that provides stability for weight‑bearing and locomotion. Understanding its bony, ligamentous and muscular architecture guides diagnosis of common low‑resource injuries and systemic diseases.

b: Synovial joint with a fibrocartilaginous labrum
Enclosed by a strong capsule reinforced by ligaments
sections.p: The hip joint connects the femoral head to the acetabulum of the pelvis, forming a synovial, diarthrodial, ball‑and‑socket joint that bears the body’s weight in standing and walking.

b: Acetabular labrum deepens socket and improves suction
Capsule attaches to the acetabular rim and intertrochanteric line
sections.p: The acetabulum is a deep, cup‑shaped socket on the lateral pelvis; the femoral head is a smooth sphere covered by articular cartilage.

b: Sciatic nerve runs posterior to joint capsule
sections.p: Anteriorly the joint lies deep to the iliopsoas tendon; posteriorly it is adjacent to the sciatic nerve and gluteal muscles; laterally the greater trochanter provides muscle leverage.

b: Medial femoral circumflex artery supplies femoral head in adults
Lateral femoral circumflex artery supplies neck and capsule
sections.p: Arterial supply comes from the medial and lateral femoral circumflex arteries (branches of the profunda femoris) and the obturator artery.

b: Pain from intra‑articular pathology often referred to groin
Posterior capsule pain may radiate to buttock
sections.p: Sensory innervation is from the femoral nerve (anterior capsule), obturator nerve (inferomedial capsule), and superior gluteal nerve (posterolateral capsule).
Allows flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and internal/external rotation; the deep socket provides stability while the surrounding muscles generate power for gait.

b: Femoral neck fracture: disrupts blood flow → risk of avascular necrosis
Posterior dislocation: often from dashboard injury, threatens sciatic nerve
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, fractures from falls or road traffic accidents, septic arthritis, and avascular necrosis (e.g., from sickle cell) are common. Understanding anatomy directs imaging, reduction, and surgical planning.

t.b: Confirms fracture pattern or dislocation; if unavailable, clinical assessment of limb length and external rotation guides urgent reduction

t.a: Ultrasound of hip (infants or septic arthritis)
t.b: Detects effusion when X‑ray is normal; if unavailable, aspirate joint if septic arthritis suspected

b: Positive Trendelenburg: weak gluteus medius, hip drops on opposite side
Pain on internal rotation with hip flexed 90° suggests intra‑articular pathology
sections.p: Key bedside maneuvers: log roll to assess pain, gait observation for Trendelenburg sign, and passive range of motion to detect restriction or instability.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hip pain with inability to bear weight after trauma
Fever, joint swelling, and limited motion suggesting septic arthritis
Progressive groin pain with limb shortening indicating possible fracture
